prompt: Each shopper wants something from an outdoor store's site. Sort each task by what serves it best.

cards.text: A first-time visitor wants to see what kinds of camping gear the store carries.
cards.explanation: Browsing a tree of parent and child categories helps a visitor orient themselves.

cards.text: A hiker wants any waterproof jacket or boot under 120 dollars, whatever its category.
cards.explanation: Waterproof rating and price cut across categories, so independent attribute filters are needed.

cards.text: A runner moves from Footwear to Running Shoes to Trail Running Shoes.
cards.explanation: Each step chooses one child of a mutually exclusive parent category.

cards.text: A shopper wants merino wool items rated four stars or more, in size M.
cards.explanation: Material, rating and size are attributes applied together to narrow the result set.

cards.text: A parent narrows 3,000 kids' items to those under 30 dollars that ship this week.
cards.explanation: Price and delivery speed are independent filters applied at the same time.

prompt: Name the job each element does on the product page of a 280-dollar office chair.

options.label: Above the fold: identity, value, action
Digital surrogate for an experience attribute

cases.text: Swatches to choose the chair's colour, next to the price and the add-to-cart button.
cases.explanation: Variant selectors belong with the title, price and call to action at the top.

cases.text: A 20-second video of someone adjusting the lumbar support and leaning back.
cases.explanation: How the chair feels when adjusted needs physical trial, so a demonstration video stands in for it.

cases.text: 'Arrives Thursday 14 May · Free returns for 100 days' printed just under the add-to-cart button.
cases.explanation: An exact delivery date and a free return window near the button counter the risk of buying unseen.

cases.text: A table of seat height range, weight capacity and foam density further down the page.
cases.explanation: Detailed technical specifications serve analytical buyers below the fold.

cases.text: A scale showing which seat width suits shoppers from 155 to 195 cm tall.
cases.explanation: A structured fit scale translates fit on different bodies into a digital form.

cases.text: '12-year warranty' badge beside the call to action.
cases.explanation: Warranty coverage next to the call to action reverses the buyer's risk.

question_text: A shoe store's week: 10,000 sessions, 6,000 product page views, 2,400 add-to-carts and 240 paid orders. Last month the same store had 2,300 add-to-carts and 920 orders. What is the most likely place to look first?
hint: Compute each step's transition rate and compare which one changed.
correct_answer_citation: Week 02 · Macro-Conversions, Micro-Conversions, and Funnel Diagnostics

options.option_text: The product thumbnails and prices on the category pages.
options.option_explanation: Category-to-product movement (60% of sessions reach a product page) is not where the change happened; add-to-carts are almost unchanged.

options.option_text: The ad campaigns bringing traffic, since the overall conversion rate is only 2.4%.
options.option_explanation: The overall rate is low, but the step-by-step rates show the loss sits after add-to-cart, not in traffic.

options.option_text: The checkout: shipping fees, forced account creation or payment errors.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Add-to-carts held steady while cart-to-order fell from about 40% to 10%, the pattern of checkout friction.

options.option_text: Nothing: micro-conversions are healthy, so the store is fine.
options.option_explanation: Micro-conversions are healthy, but the macro-conversion, the paid order, has collapsed.

prompt: Match each checkout problem with the fix that removes it.

pairs.term: A 12-dollar shipping fee appears only on the payment screen.
pairs.match: Show estimated shipping and a free-shipping progress bar on the cart page.
pairs.explanation: Upfront cost transparency removes sticker shock at the final step.

pairs.term: First-time buyers must invent a password before they can pay.
pairs.match: Offer guest checkout with only an email and an address.
pairs.explanation: Guest checkout defers account creation to the confirmation screen.

pairs.term: Phone shoppers give up while typing their street, city and postcode.
pairs.match: Use address autocomplete and a numeric keypad for the postcode.

pairs.term: Mobile buyers will not fetch their wallet to type a card number.
pairs.match: Add Apple Pay or Google Pay with fingerprint or face approval.
pairs.explanation: Digital wallets replace manual card and address entry with biometric authentication.

pairs.term: A logged-in customer leaves a full cart and closes the tab.
pairs.match: Send a reminder email within a few hours, without a discount code.
pairs.explanation: Recovery messages recapture sales; routine discounts would teach buyers to abandon on purpose.

prompt: Name the dark pattern in each storefront.

cases.text: Concert tickets advertised at 45 dollars reach 71 dollars after a 'service fee', a 'facility fee' and an 'order processing fee' appear one screen at a time.
cases.explanation: Mandatory fees are added progressively after the shopper has invested time.

cases.text: A 4-dollar 'parcel protection' line is already ticked in the cart when the shopper reaches payment.
cases.explanation: An opt-out default slips an add-on into the order without affirmative consent.

cases.text: A streaming service signs you up in one click but cancelling requires a phone call during office hours.
cases.explanation: Easy in, hard out: a roach motel.

cases.text: The pop-up's decline button reads 'No thanks, I prefer paying full price'.
cases.explanation: Emotional language on the decline button pressures the shopper.

cases.text: A 'Deal ends in 09:59' timer starts again from 10:00 every time the page is reloaded.
cases.explanation: A countdown that resets on refresh fabricates urgency.

question_text: A kettle's page shows '$39.99 · In stock · ★ 4.7 (812)' in large type, but its JSON-LD Product block contains only the name and brand. What can an AI shopping agent reading the JSON-LD verify about this kettle?
hint: JSON-LD states attribute-value pairs independent of the visual layout.
correct_answer_citation: Week 02 · Schema.org, JSON-LD, and Merchant Product Feeds

options.option_text: Only the name and the brand; the price, stock status and rating are not declared.
options.option_explanation: Correct. The block would need Offer fields (price, priceCurrency, availability) and an AggregateRating to state them.

options.option_text: Everything shown on the page, because JSON-LD copies the visible text automatically.
options.option_explanation: JSON-LD is written separately from the layout; it declares only what is put in it.

options.option_text: The price and stock status, because those are required in every Product block.
options.option_explanation: Nothing is declared unless it is written into the block.

options.option_text: Nothing at all, because agents cannot read JSON-LD.
options.option_explanation: Crawlers and agents read structured metadata blocks; this block simply says little.

prompt: Sort each storefront decision by its likely effect on an AI shopping agent that stops reading early.

bins.label: Misleads or hides from the agent

cards.text: The listing card shows price per 100 g next to the pack price.
cards.explanation: A key attribute exposed upfront on the listing card.

cards.text: A 15-dollar shipping fee appears only on the third checkout step.
cards.explanation: An unfavourable cost hidden behind later steps can lead an early-stopping agent to a dominated option.

cards.text: The blender's superior 1,500-watt motor is listed only in a downloadable PDF manual.
cards.explanation: The agent may treat the missing attribute as absent and disqualify the better product.

cards.text: Wattage, capacity and warranty appear in a visible table and in the page's JSON-LD.
cards.explanation: Upfront structured attributes for both audiences.

cards.text: A 20% restocking fee is mentioned only in a collapsed 'More policies' accordion.
cards.explanation: A penalty behind a secondary click raises acquisition cost and may never be read.

cards.text: Each product page opens with a short structured summary of size, material and returns.
cards.explanation: A structured summary lowers the cost of comparing alternatives.
